Journal-Quality Documents
A well-structured YAML for a manuscript-style document:
---
title: "Effect of Clean Fuel Intervention on Blood Pressure: A Community Trial"
author:
  - name: "Dr. Mukul Maheshwari"
    affiliation: "Department of Community Medicine"
    email: "author@institution.ac.in"
  - name: "Dr. Rudresh Negi"
    affiliation: "Department of Community Medicine"
date: today
abstract: |
  **Background:** Indoor air pollution remains a major public health concern...
  **Methods:** A cluster-randomised trial was conducted...
  **Results:** ...
  **Conclusion:** ...
keywords: [indoor air pollution, blood pressure, community trial, R]
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
    number-sections: true
    theme: flatly
  pdf:
    toc: true
    number-sections: true
    cite-method: biblatex
    pdf-engine: xelatex
    mainfont: "Times New Roman"
    fontsize: 12pt
    geometry: "margin=2.5cm"
bibliography: references.bib
csl: vancouver.csl          # citation style (download from Zotero CSL repo)
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
---

text:
Multi-File Quarto Projects

Books
A Quarto book renders multiple .qmd files into a single structured document (HTML, PDF, or ePub).
my-book/
├── _quarto.yml
├── index.qmd        (preface / front matter)
├── 01-intro.qmd
├── 02-methods.qmd
├── 03-results.qmd
├── 04-discussion.qmd
└── references.qmd
_quarto.yml for a book:
project:
  type: book

book:
  title: "Community Trial Methods in R"
  author: "Dr. Mukul Maheshwari"
  date: today
  chapters:
    - index.qmd
    - 01-intro.qmd
    - 02-methods.qmd
    - 03-results.qmd
    - 04-discussion.qmd
    - references.qmd

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
  pdf:
    documentclass: scrbook


Websites
For a multi-page website (like this workshop), see the project’s _quarto.yml for a working example of navbar configuration, profiles, and output directories.

title: Quarto — Publication
text:
GitHub + Quarto Publishing Workflow

Option A — Push rendered HTML to GitHub Pages

Render your project locally: quarto render
Output goes to docs/ (set output-dir: docs in _quarto.yml)
Commit and push the docs/ folder to GitHub
In your repository: Settings → Pages → Source → Branch: main, Folder: /docs

# Full publish cycle
quarto render
git add docs/
git commit -m "Rebuild site"
git push


Option B — GitHub Actions (automated rebuild)
Create .github/workflows/publish.yml:
name: Publish Quarto Site

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies@v2
        with:
          packages: |
            any::quarto
            any::tidyverse
            any::ggstatsplot
            any::gtsummary

      - uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2

      - name: Render and publish
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2
        with:
          target: gh-pages
With this workflow, every push to main automatically rebuilds and deploys the site.


Option C — Quarto Pub (zero configuration)
quarto publish quarto-pub
Creates a free public site at username.quarto.pub/project-name. Suitable for sharing documents without managing a GitHub repository.

Embedding Shiny in Quarto
For lightweight interactivity within a static Quarto document.

Using shinylive (no server required)
shinylive compiles Shiny to WebAssembly — no Shiny server needed.
---
title: "Interactive Report"
format: html
filters:
  - shinylive
---
```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
library(shiny)
library(ggplot2)

ui <- fluidPage(
  sliderInput("bins", "Bins:", 5, 50, 20),
  plotOutput("hist")
)

server <- function(input, output) {
  output$hist <- renderPlot({
    ggplot(data.frame(x = rnorm(500)), aes(x)) +
      geom_histogram(bins = input$bins)
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```
Install shinylive:
install.packages("shinylive")
quarto::quarto_add_extension("quarto-ext/shinylive")


Embedding a deployed Shiny app with <iframe>
If you have an app on shinyapps.io:
<iframe src="https://yourname.shinyapps.io/yourapp/"
        width="100%" height="600px"
        style="border: none;">
</iframe>

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
ggwithinstats() — Repeated Measures
Use this when the same participants are measured more than once (paired/within-subjects design) — for example, pre-post measurements.

library(ggstatsplot)
library(tidyr)

# Reshape from wide to long for within-subjects comparison
overall_long <- overall_up |>
  select(member_id, sbp_0m, sbp_3m) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(sbp_0m, sbp_3m),
    names_to  = "timepoint",
    values_to = "sbp"
  ) |>
  mutate(timepoint = factor(timepoint,
                            levels = c("sbp_0m", "sbp_3m"),
                            labels = c("Baseline", "3 Months")))

ggwithinstats(
  data    = overall_long,
  x       = timepoint,
  y       = sbp,
  subject.id = member_id,       # links pairs across timepoints
  title   = "Systolic BP: Baseline vs 3 Months"
)

Key differences from ggbetweenstats():

subject.id is required — it tells the function which rows are paired
Uses a paired t-test (parametric) or Wilcoxon signed-rank (non-parametric)
Lines connect paired observations in the plot

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
ggbarstats() — Proportions
Use this when you want to compare proportions of a categorical outcome across groups. The output includes a χ² or Fisher’s exact test.

ggbarstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = fuel_type,           # grouping variable (x-axis)
  y     = tobacco_type,        # outcome category (fill)
  title = "Tobacco Type by Fuel Type"
)

What the output shows:

Stacked bar chart with proportion labels
χ² test statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and Cramér’s V effect size
Pairwise comparisons between bars (if > 2 groups)

Swap axes to change orientation:

# Make tobacco_type the grouping variable
ggbarstats(data = overall_up, x = tobacco_type, y = fuel_type)

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
ggpiestats() — Pie / Donut Charts
Use this for a single categorical variable, or two categorical variables where a pie chart is appropriate for the audience.

# Single variable — proportions of intervention types
ggpiestats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = intervention,
  title = "Distribution of Intervention Groups"
)


# Two variables — tobacco type by intervention
ggpiestats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = tobacco_type,
  y     = intervention,       # creates faceted pies
  title = "Tobacco Type by Intervention"
)







WarningWhen to use pie charts



Pie charts are appropriate when there are ≤ 5 categories and the audience is non-technical. For more categories or detailed comparisons, prefer ggbarstats().

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
Customising appearance
All ggstatsplot functions return a ggplot2 object, so you can extend them normally.

library(ggplot2)

ggbetweenstats(
  data        = overall_up,
  x           = fuel_type,
  y           = sbp_0m,
  # Colours for each group
  palette     = "Set2",
  package     = "RColorBrewer",
  # Remove the subtitle (statistical results) if preferred
  results.subtitle = TRUE,
  # Change point size and transparency
  point.args  = list(size = 2, alpha = 0.4),
  title       = "Systolic BP by Fuel Type"
) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  labs(caption = "Source: NCTOH Study Dataset")

What it controls

Colour palette for groups


results.subtitle

text:
Introduction to Bayes Factors
When you set type = "bayes", ggstatsplot reports a Bayes Factor (BF₁₀) instead of a p-value.

ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = fuel_type,
  y     = sbp_0m,
  type  = "bayes",
  title = "Systolic BP by Fuel Type (Bayesian)"
)

Interpreting BF₁₀:



BF₁₀
Interpretation




> 100
Extreme evidence for H₁


30–100
Very strong evidence for H₁


10–30
Strong evidence for H₁


3–10
Moderate evidence for H₁


1–3
Anecdotal evidence for H₁


~1
No evidence either way


1/3–1
Anecdotal evidence for H₀


< 1/10
Strong–extreme evidence for H₀




BF₁₀ > 3: reasonably confident that H₁ (an effect exists) is supported
BF₁₀ < 1/3: reasonably confident that H₀ (no effect) is supported
Values between 1/3 and 3 are inconclusive







Note



Bayesian inference and deeper interpretation of Bayes factors is covered in ggstatsplot — Advanced.

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
Bayesian Reporting Workflow
The Bayesian approach in ggstatsplot uses the BayesFactor package internally. The goal is to quantify how much evidence exists for or against an effect, rather than simply crossing a significance threshold.

Setting priors

library(ggstatsplot)

# Default Cauchy prior (r = 0.707) — appropriate for most comparisons
ggbetweenstats(
  data         = overall_up,
  x            = intervention,
  y            = sbp_0m,
  type         = "bayes",
  bf.prior     = 0.707,        # scale of Cauchy prior on effect size
  title        = "SBP by Intervention (Bayesian, default prior)"
)

# Narrow prior — use if you expect a small effect
ggbetweenstats(
  data         = overall_up,
  x            = intervention,
  y            = sbp_0m,
  type         = "bayes",
  bf.prior     = 0.5,
  title        = "SBP by Intervention (narrow prior)"
)



Reporting Bayes factors in text
When BF₁₀ = 18.4:

“A Bayesian independent-samples t-test revealed moderate-to-strong evidence for a difference in baseline SBP between intervention groups, BF₁₀ = 18.4, δ = 0.41, 95% credible interval [0.18, 0.65].”

When BF₁₀ = 0.21:

“A Bayesian independent-samples t-test provided moderate evidence in favour of the null hypothesis (no difference in SBP), BF₁₀ = 0.21.”







TipKey distinction: BF₁₀ vs BF₀₁




BF₁₀: evidence for H₁ over H₀ (use when testing for an effect)
BF₀₁ = 1/BF₁₀: evidence for H₀ over H₁ (use when supporting the null)

ggstatsplot reports BF₁₀ by default. To interpret support for H₀, invert it.

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
grouped_* Functions — Faceted Comparisons
The grouped_* variants run the same comparison separately within each level of a grouping variable and combine the results into a faceted plot.

# Compare SBP across tobacco types, separately by sex
grouped_ggbetweenstats(
  data             = overall_up,
  x                = tobacco_type,
  y                = sbp_0m,
  grouping.var     = sex,           # one panel per sex
  title            = "SBP by Tobacco Type, stratified by Sex",
  plotgrid.args    = list(ncol = 2)
)


# Correlation stratified by intervention group
grouped_ggscatterstats(
  data         = overall_up,
  x            = current_age,
  y            = sbp_0m,
  grouping.var = intervention,
  title        = "Age vs SBP by Intervention Group"
)

ggcorrmat() — Correlation Matrix
Visualises pairwise correlations across multiple continuous variables with significance annotations.

ggcorrmat(
  data   = overall_up |> select(current_age, sbp_0m, sbp_3m, sbp_6m,
                                 consumption_per_day_0m),
  title  = "Correlation Matrix — Baseline Variables",
  type   = "parametric"     # "parametric", "nonparametric", "robust", "bayes"
)

Method
When to use

text:
Combining with patchwork
All ggstatsplot outputs are ggplot2 objects and compose naturally with patchwork.

library(patchwork)

p1 <- ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = intervention,
  y     = sbp_0m,
  title = "Baseline SBP"
)

p2 <- ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = intervention,
  y     = sbp_3m,
  title = "3-Month SBP"
)

p3 <- ggscatterstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = sbp_0m,
  y     = sbp_3m,
  title = "Baseline vs 3-Month SBP"
)

# Compose: two plots on top, one full-width below
(p1 | p2) / p3 +
  plot_annotation(
    title   = "Blood Pressure Outcomes by Intervention",
    caption = "Source: NCTOH Study Dataset"
  )

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
Publication-ready output

library(ggplot2)

pub_plot <- ggbetweenstats(
  data             = overall_up,
  x                = intervention,
  y                = sbp_0m,
  type             = "parametric",
  pairwise.display = "significant",    # show only significant comparisons
  p.adjust.method  = "bonferroni",
  title            = "Baseline Systolic Blood Pressure by Intervention Group",
  xlab             = "Intervention Group",
  ylab             = "Systolic BP (mmHg)",
  package          = "RColorBrewer",
  palette          = "Set1"
) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.line        = element_line(linewidth = 0.5),
    plot.caption     = element_text(hjust = 0, colour = "grey50")
  ) +
  labs(caption = "Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons shown for p < 0.05")

# Save at print quality
ggsave("figures/sbp_by_intervention.png",
       pub_plot, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300)

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
Case Study: Healthcare Data
A complete example using the NCTOH study dataset — comparing the change in SBP across intervention groups, accounting for tobacco type.

library(ggstatsplot)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)

# Derive SBP change variable
study_data <- overall_up |>
  mutate(sbp_change = sbp_3m - sbp_0m)

# 1. Overall change by intervention
p_overall <- ggbetweenstats(
  data  = study_data,
  x     = intervention,
  y     = sbp_change,
  type  = "parametric",
  title = "Change in SBP at 3 Months"
)

# 2. Stratified by tobacco type
p_strat <- grouped_ggbetweenstats(
  data         = study_data,
  x            = intervention,
  y            = sbp_change,
  grouping.var = tobacco_type,
  title        = "SBP Change Stratified by Tobacco Type",
  plotgrid.args = list(ncol = 3)
)

# View each
p_overall
p_strat

title: Exporting plots
text: Exporting plots from R can be done in several ways, depending on the desired output format and quality. Here are some common methods to export plots:

title: Exporting plots
text:
Using R’s Built-in Functions
R provides several built-in functions for exporting plots to different formats:

Raster Formats

png(), jpeg(), tiff(), bmp(): These functions save plots in raster formats. You can specify filename, dimensions, and resolution.

# PNG format (good for web)
png("plot.png", width = 800, height = 600, res = 100)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()

# High-resolution TIFF for publications
tiff("plot.tiff", width = 8, height = 6, units = "in", res = 300)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()


Vector Formats

pdf(): Saves plots in PDF format, vector-based and scalable.
svg(): Saves plots in SVG format, ideal for web and scalable graphics.

# PDF for high-quality prints
pdf("plot.pdf", width = 8, height = 6)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()

# SVG for web use
svg("plot.svg", width = 8, height = 6)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()

title: Exporting plots
text:
Exporting ggplot2 Plots
For ggplot2 plots, the ggsave() function is the most convenient way to export:
library(ggplot2)

# Create a plot
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point()

# Save in different formats
ggsave("plot.png", p, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 150)
ggsave("plot.pdf", p, width = 8, height = 6)
ggsave("plot.svg", p, width = 8, height = 6)

Controlling Output Quality

Resolution (DPI): Higher DPI for print quality (300+), lower for web (72-150)
Dimensions: Specify in inches or pixels
Aspect Ratio: Maintain proportions for consistency

# High-resolution for publications
ggsave("publication_plot.tiff", p, 
       width = 6, height = 4, 
       dpi = 300, 
       device = "tiff")

# Web-optimized PNG
ggsave("web_plot.png", p, 
       width = 800, height = 600, 
       dpi = 100, 
       units = "px")

title: Exporting plots
text:
Advanced Exporting Techniques

Exporting Multiple Plots
# Save multiple plots to PDF
pdf("multiple_plots.pdf")

print(plot1)
plot2 <- ggplot(data2, aes(x, y)) + geom_line()
print(plot2)

Using Cairo for Better Quality
The Cairo graphics library can provide better quality for some formats:
install.packages("Cairo")
library(Cairo)

CairoPNG("high_quality.png", width = 800, height = 600)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()


Exporting to Clipboard
For quick sharing:
# Windows
savePlot("clipboard", type = "wmf")

# Or for ggplot2
ggsave("clipboard", p, device = "png")

title: Exporting plots
text:
Best Practices

Choose the right format: PDF/SVG for vector graphics, PNG/TIFF for raster
Set appropriate resolution: 300 DPI for print, 72-150 for screen
Consider file size: Vector formats scale better but may be larger
Test outputs: Always check exported files in target applications
Use consistent dimensions: Maintain aspect ratios across exports

title: Exporting plots
text:
Common Issues and Solutions

Plot not saving: Ensure dev.off() is called after plotting
Low quality: Increase DPI or use vector formats
Wrong dimensions: Specify units explicitly (inches, cm, pixels)
Colors not matching: Check color profiles and device settings

title: Advanced Exporting Techniques
text:
This chapter covers advanced techniques for exporting plots, including programmatic generation, batch processing, custom devices, and integration with other tools.




library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)

# Create plots for each cylinder group
plots <- mtcars %>%
  split(.$cyl) %>%
  map(~ ggplot(.x, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + 
        geom_point() + 
        ggtitle(paste("Cylinders:", .x$cyl[1])))

# Save each plot
walk2(plots, names(plots), 
      ~ ggsave(filename = paste0("plot_cyl_", .x, ".png"), 
               plot = .y, 
               width = 6, height = 4))



# Generate timestamped filenames
timestamp <- format(Sys.time(), "%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")

ggsave(paste0("analysis_plot_", timestamp, ".pdf"), 
       plot = p, 
       width = 8, height = 6)






save_plot_multiple_formats <- function(plot, filename_base, 
                                     formats = c("png", "pdf", "svg")) {
  for (fmt in formats) {
    filename <- paste0(filename_base, ".", fmt)
    ggsave(filename, plot, width = 8, height = 6)
  }
}

# Usage
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
save_plot_multiple_formats(p, "mtcars_scatter")



datasets <- list(
  mtcars = mtcars,
  iris = iris,
  airquality = airquality
)

for (name in names(datasets)) {
  data <- datasets[[name]]
  # Create appropriate plot based on data
  if (name == "mtcars") {
    p <- ggplot(data, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
  } else if (name == "iris") {
    p <- ggplot(data, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width, color = Species)) + 
      geom_point()
  }
  
  ggsave(paste0(name, "_plot.png"), p, width = 6, height = 4)
}






library(Cairo)

# High-quality PNG
CairoPNG("high_quality.png", width = 800, height = 600, 
         bg = "white", pointsize = 12)
plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
dev.off()

# PDF with embedded fonts
CairoPDF("embedded_fonts.pdf", width = 8, height = 6, 
         family = "Arial")
plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
dev.off()



# Create a custom device wrapper
save_high_res <- function(filename, plot_func, ...) {
  png(filename, width = 1200, height = 800, res = 150, ...)
  plot_func()
  dev.off()
}

# Usage
my_plot <- function() {
  plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg, 
       xlab = "Weight", ylab = "MPG",
       main = "High Resolution Plot")
}

save_high_res("high_res_plot.png", my_plot)






library(tikzDevice)

# Export as TikZ for LaTeX
tikz("plot.tex", width = 4, height = 3)
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
dev.off()



# Export as HTML with plotly
library(plotly)
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(ggplotly(p), "interactive_plot.html")






# Create publication-ready theme

# Load data with all transformations
bp_data <- read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx") %>%
  mutate(
    SysBP_Change = SysBP_6m - SysBP_0m,
    DiaBP_Change = DiaBP_6m - DiaBP_0m,
    AgeGroup = cut(Age, breaks = c(0, 30, 50, 65, 100),
                   labels = c("18-30", "31-50", "51-65", "65+")),
    Hypertension_Baseline = ifelse(SysBP_0m >= 140 | DiaBP_0m >= 90, 
                                   "Hypertensive", "Normal"),
    BMI_Category = cut(BMI, breaks = c(0, 18.5, 25, 30, 100),
                       labels = c("Underweight", "Normal", "Overweight", "Obese"))
  )

# Time series
bp_time <- bp_data %>%
  select(PatientID, TreatmentGroup, SysBP_0m, SysBP_3m, SysBP_6m) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("SysBP"),
               names_to = "Time", values_to = "SysBP") %>%
  mutate(Months = as.numeric(gsub("SysBP_|m", "", Time)))

# Summary data
bp_summary <- bp_time %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup, Months) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ci_data <- bp_time %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup, Months) %>%
  summarise(Mean = mean(SysBP), SE = sd(SysBP) / sqrt(n()), .groups = "drop")

# Custom theme from Module 3
theme_clinical_report <- function(base_size = 12, base_family = "serif") {
  theme_bw(base_size = base_size, base_family = base_family) +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = base_family),
    plot.title = element_text(size = base_size * 1.3, face = "bold", 
                              hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = base_size * 1.1, hjust = 0.5,
                                 color = "gray30", margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9, hjust = 1,
                                face = "italic", color = "gray50"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = base_size * 1.1, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9, color = "gray20"),
    axis.line = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "gray90", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "gray40", fill = NA, linewidth = 1),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(size = base_size, face = "bold"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    legend.key = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)
  )
}

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 4

Common Pitfalls to Avoid

Mapping constants inside aes() - Use fixed values outside aes
Too many aesthetics - Limit to 3-4 visual encodings max
Poor color choices - Always test for colorblind accessibility
Overplotting - Use alpha, jitter, or facets
Misleading axes - Always start at zero for bar charts
Too much clutter - Remove unnecessary grid lines, legends, or decorations
Inconsistent themes - Use theme_set() for consistency
Ignoring aspect ratios - Consider final output dimensions
Not saving properly - Use appropriate format and resolution
Forgetting reproducibility - Set seed, document packages

Best Practices Checklist
Before finalizing visualizations:

Color: Use colorblind-friendly palettes (viridis, ColorBrewer)
Contrast: Ensure sufficient contrast between elements
Text size: Minimum 10pt for body text, 12pt+ for titles
Redundancy: Don’t rely on color alone (use shape, pattern, labels)
Simplicity: Remove unnecessary elements
Labels: Clear, descriptive axis labels and titles
Alt text: Provide text description for screen readers
Print: Test in grayscale/black & white
Simulation: Test with colorblind simulator
Font: Use readable fonts (avoid decorative fonts)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 4

  geom_point(aes(color = var3, size = var4)) +     # 2. Geometry + Local aes
  scale_color_viridis_d() +                        # 3. Scales
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 6)) +         # 4. More scales
  facet_wrap(~ var5) +                             # 5. Facets
  labs(title = "My Plot",                          # 6. Labels
       x = "X Label", y = "Y Label") +
  theme_minimal() +                                # 7. Theme

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 4
text:
Key Takeaways

Grammar of Graphics provides a systematic framework for building visualizations
Layering is fundamental - data → aesthetics → geometries → scales → themes
Aesthetics map data to visual properties (inside aes())
Geoms are the building blocks - choose appropriately for your data type
Themes control appearance - use built-in or create custom ones
Colors matter - always consider colorblind accessibility
Scales control how data maps to aesthetics - customize breaks, limits, labels
Facets enable small multiples for comparing groups
Consistency is key - use global themes and organizational standards
Know ggplot2’s limitations and when to use alternatives

library(ggplot2)

library(tidyr)
library(readxl)
library(ggthemes)  # For additional themes

# Load and prepare data
bp_data <- read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx") %>%
  mutate(
    SysBP_Change = SysBP_6m - SysBP_0m,
    AgeGroup = cut(Age, breaks = c(0, 30, 50, 65, 100),
                   labels = c("18-30", "31-50", "51-65", "65+")),
    Hypertension_Baseline = ifelse(SysBP_0m >= 140 | DiaBP_0m >= 90, 
                                   "Hypertensive", "Normal"),
    BMI_Category = cut(BMI, breaks = c(0, 18.5, 25, 30, 100),
                       labels = c("Underweight", "Normal", "Overweight", "Obese"))
  )

# Time series data
bp_time <- bp_data %>%
  select(PatientID, TreatmentGroup, SysBP_0m, SysBP_3m, SysBP_6m) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("SysBP"),
               names_to = "Time", values_to = "SysBP") %>%
  mutate(Months = as.numeric(gsub("SysBP_|m", "", Time)))

bp_summary <- bp_time %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup, Months) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Global vs Local Aesthetics

Global aesthetics: Defined in ggplot(), apply to all layers
Local aesthetics: Defined in geom_*(), apply to specific layer
Local aesthetics override global aesthetics
Use global for shared mappings, local for layer-specific mappings



Code
ggplot(data, aes(x = var1, y = var2)) +          # Global
  geom_point(aes(color = var3)) +                 # Local (adds color)
  geom_smooth()                                   # Uses global only

       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m,

  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

● Gold/Yellow = Distribution - Shows data spread, frequency, shape, outliers

├── Numeric → Histogram, Density, Boxplot

├── Numeric × Numeric → Scatter, Hexbin, Bubble

├── Numeric × Numeric × Numeric → Bubble, Faceted Scatter

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution | ● Ranking | ● Part of Whole
Chart Options:

Bar Chart ● (counts/frequencies)
Lollipop Chart ● (alternative to bar, especially for long lists)
Cleveland Dot Plot ● (ranked comparison)
Pie Chart ● (≤5 categories only, part-to-whole)
Doughnut Chart ● (like pie, better labels)
Circular Bar Plot ● (aesthetic alternative)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease prevalence by state
Hospitalization by insurance type
Comorbidity frequency distribution

Decision Guide:

Few categories (<5) and need part-of-whole → Pie/Doughnut
Few-moderate categories → Bar chart (horizontal if long names)
Many categories (>8) → Lollipop or Cleveland dot
Need ranking emphasis → Ordered bar or lollipop

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution | ● Part of Whole (Ordered)
Chart Options:

Ordered Bar Chart ● (maintain categorical order)
Ordered Dot Plot ●
Cumulative Frequency Plot ● (especially for Likert scales)
Frequency Polygon ● (smooth trend)

Healthcare Examples:

Patient satisfaction (Likert: 1=Very Unsatisfied to 5=Very Satisfied)
Tumor stages frequency (Stage I → II → III → IV)
Pain severity distribution (None → Mild → Moderate → Severe)
Risk level counts (Low → Medium → High)

Decision Guide:

Likert scales → Stacked ordered bar or cumulative frequency
Natural progression (stages, severity) → Maintain order on axis
Show accumulation → Cumulative frequency plot
Compare between groups → Grouped ordered bar

title: Navigating the Decision Tree

Chart Options:

Histogram ● (shows bin structure, distribution shape)
Density Plot ● (smooth, continuous estimate)
Boxplot ● (summary: median, quartiles, outliers)
Violin Plot ● (distribution + boxplot combined)
Dot/Strip Plot ● (individual points, best for small n)

Healthcare Examples:

Age distribution in cohort
Blood pressure measurements in population
Lab values (HbA1c, cholesterol, creatinine)
Hospital length of stay

Decision Guide:



Scenario
Best Choice
Why




n < 20
Dot/Strip plot
See every point


n = 20-100
Histogram + Boxplot
Balance detail & summary


n > 100
Density plot
Smooth, reduces noise


Want outliers
Boxplot
Shows extreme values clearly


Want shape details
Violin plot
Shows multimodality, skewness

text:
● Evolution
Chart Options:

Line Chart ● (standard for continuous time data)
Area Chart ● (emphasizes magnitude/volume)
Streamgraph ● (stacked area with flowing theme)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease incidence trends over years
Hospital admission rates monthly
COVID-19 case counts by week
Patient vital signs during hospitalization

Decision Guide:

Single series, continuous time → Line chart
Show cumulative volume → Area chart
Multiple series, show total → Stacked area
Sparse time points → Line chart with markers

title: Navigating the Decision Tree

● Maps
Chart Options:

Choropleth Map ● (color-coded by region)
Bubble Map ● (circles sized by value)
Heat Map ● (geographic intensity)
Dot Map ● (point locations)

Healthcare Examples:

Regional disease rates (e.g., TB incidence by state in India)
Hospital bed density by district
Maternal mortality ratios by region
Vaccination coverage by area

Decision Guide:

Show rate/percentage by region → Choropleth
Show absolute counts by location → Bubble map
Show intensity/density → Heat map
Specific point locations matter → Dot map

Scenario
Best Choice

Sample Size
Distribution Focus
Summary Focus




n < 30

n = 30-100

Chart Options:

Logistic Regression Curve ● (smooth probability line)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution (Ordered)
Chart Options:

Ordered Boxplot ● (boxplot by ordinal groups, maintaining order)
Ordered Violin Plot ● (violin by ordinal groups)
Ordered Jittered Points ● (points by group, groups ordered)

Healthcare Examples:

Medication efficacy vs dose level (Low/Medium/High)
Lab value vs disease severity (Stage I-IV)
Pain score vs treatment intensity (Mild/Moderate/Severe)
Functional status vs age group (Young/Middle/Elderly)

Key Point:

Always maintain explicit ordering on axis
Example: Severity I → II → III → IV (not random order)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Evolution | ● Correlation (Trend)
Chart Options:

Line Chart ● (single series over time)
Multi-line Chart ● (multiple series overlay)
Area Chart ● (cumulative volume over time)
Stacked Area Chart ● (composition over time)
Connected Scatter ● (if sparse time points)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease incidence trends over years (single disease)
Patient vital signs over hospital stay (temperature, BP, HR)
Medication effectiveness over weeks (Drug A vs B)
Mortality rates over decades by region

Decision Guide:

Single series → Line chart
Few series (2-3) to compare → Multi-line chart
Many series, want to show total → Stacked area
Series showing parts of whole → Stacked area
Sparse measurements → Line with markers or connected scatter

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Evolution (By Group) | ● Correlation (Group Comparison)
Chart Options:

Grouped Line Chart ● (separate lines for each group)
Faceted Line Chart ● (separate subplots per group)
Grouped Area Chart ● (stacked or overlapping)
Interaction Plot ● (lines intersecting showing interaction)
Ribbon Chart ● (flowing bands representing groups)

Healthcare Examples:

Mortality rate trends (gender comparison: M vs F)
Hospital admission trends by institution (5-year follow-up)
Drug effectiveness over time by treatment arm
Complication rates by age group over study period

Decision Guide:

Few groups (2-3) → Multi-line chart
Many groups (5+) → Faceted line plots
Want to show total + groups → Stacked area
Interaction patterns matter → Interaction plot (lines cross)
Space constraints → Faceting better than overlapping

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution (Ordered) | ● Part of Whole (Ordered)
Chart Options:

Ordered Grouped Bar Chart ● (bars by category, groups ordered)
Ordered Stacked Bar ● (stacked, ordinal categories in order)
Faceted Ordered Bar ● (subplots maintaining order)

Healthcare Examples:

Patient satisfaction (Likert: 1-5) by hospital ward
Pain severity (None/Mild/Moderate/Severe) by treatment type
Risk level (Low/Med/High) by comorbidity count
Functional status by treatment arm

Key Point:

Maintain ordinal ordering on one axis
Example: Satisfaction scale always: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
3+ Continuous Variables | ● Correlation
Chart Options:

Bubble Plot ● (x, y, size = 3rd; color/opacity = 4th)
Faceted Scatter ● (scatter by groups, multiple subplots)
3D Scatter (NOT recommended: distorts perception)

Healthcare Examples:

Age vs BMI (size=cholesterol, color=treatment arm)
HbA1c vs glucose (size=insulin, faceted by gender)
Systolic vs diastolic BP (colored by smoking status)

Decision Guide:

3 variables → Bubble plot (x, y, size)
4 variables → Bubble + color
5+ variables → Multiple faceted plots (don’t try to cram)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Correlation Matrix
Chart Options:

Correlation Matrix ● (numeric table of coefficients)
Correlogram ● (heatmap with color intensity = correlation strength)
Scatter Plot Matrix ● (pairwise scatter plots)

Healthcare Examples:

Lab inter-correlations: glucose, insulin, triglycerides, HDL, LDL
Vital signs correlations: BP, HR, RR, O2 saturation, temperature
Biomarker relationships in cohort study

Visualization:

Color intensity (warm = positive, cool = negative)
Cell size may represent correlation strength
Diagonal typically = 1.0 (variable with itself)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution (Faceted) | ● Correlation (Interaction)
Chart Options:

Faceted Boxplot/Violin ● (boxplot per group, subplots for 3rd variable)
Interaction Plot ● (lines connecting means by two factors)
Faceted Scatter + regression lines ● (by groups)

Healthcare Examples:

HbA1c by treatment type, faceted by gender (4 subplots: 2 treat × 2 gender)
Lab values by disease status, colored by age group
Drug efficacy by dose level, faceted by patient comorbidity

Visualization Strategy:

Primary grouping on axis
Secondary grouping via facets or colors
Show interactions: do lines cross? Do patterns differ?

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Evolution (Advanced) | ● Distribution (Temporal)
Chart Options:

Multi-line Chart with Faceting ● (separate subplots per group)
Ridgeline Plot ● (distribution by group, stacked vertically)
Slope Chart ● (start → end values, multiple series)
Animated Time Series ● (interactive exploration)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease incidence over years, separate lines by region (5 regions)
Patient vitals during admission, faceted by treatment arm
Hospital census by time, colored by department

Decision Guide:

Multiple time series + groups → Faceted multi-line
Distribution evolution over time → Ridgeline plot
Show change from start to end → Slope chart

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Flow | ● Part of Whole (Hierarchical)
Chart Options:

Sankey Diagram ● (flow from one category to another)
Alluvial Diagram ● (similar to Sankey, broader flows)
Treemap ● (nested rectangles for hierarchy)
Sunburst Chart ● (nested circles/rings for hierarchy)

Healthcare Examples:

Sankey: Patient flow (admission → diagnostic → treatment → discharge)
Alluvial: Disease progression stages (diagnosis → worsening/improvement → outcome)
Treemap: Hospital structure (Region → Hospital → Department → Ward)
Sunburst: Disease classification (Category → Subcategory → Specific condition)

Decision Guide:

Flow/transition/journey → Sankey or Alluvial
Nested hierarchy/parts → Treemap or Sunburst

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Flow | ● Correlation (Connections)
Chart Options:

Sankey Diagram ● (directional flows between nodes)
Chord Diagram ● (bi-directional relationships, circular)
Network Graph ● (nodes + edges, force-directed layout)
Arc Diagram ● (nodes in line, arcs show connections)

Healthcare Examples:

Sankey: Patient journeys through clinic system
Chord: Disease co-occurrence patterns (patient network)
Network: Hospital referral patterns (which hospitals refer to which)
Arc: Comorbidity networks (which diseases co-occur)

Visualization:

Nodes = entities (patients, diseases, hospitals)
Edges/arcs/flows = relationships (referral, co-occurrence)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Part of Whole | ● Flow
Chart Options:

Treemap ● (nested rectangles, size ∝ value)
Sunburst Chart ● (nested circles, size ∝ value)
Hierarchical Edge Bundling ● (connections in hierarchy)

Healthcare Examples:

Treemap: Hospital admissions by Region → State → Hospital → Department (size = admission count)
Sunburst: Disease classification by Category → Subcategory → Specific condition → ICD code
Hierarchical Edge Bundling: Referral patterns between hospitals at different levels

Decision Guide:

Static hierarchy focus → Treemap
Want circular aesthetic → Sunburst
Complex relationships in hierarchy → Hierarchical edge bundling

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
❌ What NOT to Do
❌ Pie charts with 10+ categories

Why? Human perception fails with small angles
Solution: Use bar chart ●, lollipop ●, or split into multiple pies

❌ 3D charts

Why? Perspective distorts data perception (3D cone/pyramid/sphere)
Solution: Stick to 2D representations

❌ Dual-axis charts

Why? Can mislead by manipulating axis scales
Solution: Use faceting or separate plots instead

❌ Wrong color coding

Why? Color should reinforce analytical goal (not random aesthetic)
Solution: Sequential colors for magnitude, categorical colors for groups

❌ Overplotting (overlapping points)

Why? Can’t see density or exact position
Solution: Use transparency (alpha), jitter, hexbin ●, or density plots ●

❌ Stacked bars for detailed comparison

Why? Only first and last categories are easy to compare
Solution: Use grouped bar ● or faceting for detailed comparison

❌ Too many dimensions on one plot

Why? Cognitive overload, hard to extract insight
Solution: Split into multiple focused visualizations

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
Core Principles for Effective Visualization
✅ Always start with your analytical goal - What question are you answering? (distribute, compare, rank, relate, etc.)
✅ Data types narrow your options significantly - Numeric vs Categoric vs Ordinal vs Temporal vs Spatial
✅ Multiple valid charts may exist—choose based on audience & context - Scientist ≠ Executive ≠ Patient communication
✅ Use color strategically to support your analytical goal - Sequential for magnitude, categorical for groups, diverging for contrasts
✅ Simplicity trumps complexity; avoid unnecessary dimensions - If 3D doesn’t add insight, keep it 2D - If faceting helps clarity, use it
✅ When in doubt, check data-to-viz.com or reference examples - Don’t reinvent the wheel; learn from established best practices
✅ Practice makes perfect—iterate on visualizations - First draft rarely optimal; refine based on feedback

title: Best Practices
text:
Introduction to Data Visualization

“The simple graph has brought more information to the data analyst’s mind than any other device.” - John Tukey


Data visualization transforms complex data into visual insights
Good visualizations tell a story
Poor visualizations mislead or confuse
Every choice matters - especially in healthcare

title: Best Practices
text:
The Big Idea
Can you summarize your message in one sentence?

Your “Big Idea” should be:

Articulate your point of view: What do you want your audience to know?
Convey what’s at stake: Why does this matter?
Be a complete sentence: Not just a topic, but a statement

Example: “We should implement early discharge planning because it reduces readmissions by 35%”

title: Best Practices
section: Principle 1: Choose the Right Chart Type
text:
Principle 1: Choose the Right Chart Type
Match your visualization to your data and message
Different types of data require different visualizations:

Simple text: 1-2 key numbers
Tables: Multiple precise values
Categorical: Bar charts (horizontal preferred)
Continuous over time: Line charts, area charts
Distributions: Histograms, boxplots, violin plots, density plots
Relationships: Scatter plots, correlations
Comparisons: Slopegraphs, small multiples
Part-to-whole: Stacked bars (avoid pie charts)

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Simple Text


Effective: When you have just 1-2 key numbers, text is more impactful than a chart. Makes the metric impossible to miss and allows for immediate comprehension.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Table


Effective: Tables excel when precise values matter and units differ. Better than charts when readers need exact numbers for comparison or reference.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Heatmap


Effective: Heatmaps encode values with color, making patterns instantly visible in large tables. Ideal for spotting trends across two categorical dimensions.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Horizontal Bar Chart


Effective: Horizontal bars are preferred for categorical comparisons. Long labels read naturally, and length comparisons are easier than height comparisons.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Grouped Bar Chart


Effective: Grouped bars allow direct comparison across two categorical variables. The gap between groups creates visual separation that aids comprehension.

title: Best Practices
section: Avoid: Vertical Bars with Long Labels
text:
Avoid: Vertical Bars with Long Labels


Ineffective: Vertical bars with long labels force text rotation, making reading difficult. Horizontal bars solve this problem naturally.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Line Chart


Effective: Line charts emphasize continuity and trend direction over time. The connecting line helps viewers see patterns and predict future values.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Area Chart


Effective: Stacked area charts show both individual trends and cumulative total. The filled areas emphasize volume and make the overall trend prominent.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Multiple Line Series


Effective: Multiple series work when normalized to comparable scales. Different colors distinguish series while the shared timeline enables pattern comparison across variables.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Scatter Plot


Effective: Scatter plots reveal relationships between continuous variables. The trend line and confidence interval quantify the strength and uncertainty of the relationship.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Scatter with Categories


Effective: Adding categories to scatter plots reveals whether relationships hold across subgroups. Parallel slopes suggest consistent effects; diverging slopes indicate interactions.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Boxplot


Effective: Boxplots show distribution shape through quartiles. The box contains 50% of data, whiskers show range, and outliers appear as points - all in one compact visual.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Violin Plot


Effective: Violin plots reveal distribution details that boxplots hide. The width at each point shows density, making bimodal distributions and skewness immediately apparent.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Density Plot


Effective: Density plots show smooth distribution curves, ideal for comparing shapes between groups. Overlapping areas make differences in location, spread, and skewness clear.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Ridgeline Plot


Effective: Ridgeline plots stack density curves for easy comparison across many categories. The slight overlap creates visual flow while maintaining distinct distributions.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Slopegraph


Effective: Slopegraphs excel at showing change between two time points. The slope angle immediately conveys magnitude and direction of change for each entity.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Stacked Bar Chart


Effective: Stacked bars show part-to-whole relationships over time. Total height shows cumulative volume while segment heights reveal individual contributions.

title: Best Practices
section: Avoid: Y-Axis Not Starting at Zero
text:
Avoid: Y-Axis Not Starting at Zero


Ineffective: Truncating the Y-axis on bar charts distorts proportional relationships. What is actually a 3% difference appears as a 3-fold difference due to the missing baseline.

title: Best Practices
text:
Better: Y-Axis Starting at Zero


Effective: Starting bar charts at zero shows true proportions. Now it’s clear that all hospitals perform similarly at high levels with minimal variation.

title: Best Practices
text:
Avoid: Pie Charts


Ineffective: Humans struggle with angle and area estimation. Quick: is Respiratory or Other larger? Pie charts make simple comparisons unnecessarily difficult.

title: Best Practices
text:
Better: Horizontal Bar Chart


Effective: Horizontal bars make comparisons effortless. Rankings are immediately clear, and length differences are precisely perceivable unlike angles in pie charts.

title: Best Practices
text:
Principle 2: Eliminate Clutter
Remove anything that doesn’t add value

Remove chart borders and backgrounds
Lighten or remove gridlines

Remove redundant data labels
Direct labeling > legends (Gestalt principle of connection)
Clean up axis labels
Maximize data-to-ink ratio (Tufte’s principle)

title: Best Practices
text:
Data-to-Ink Ratio: Maximizing Information
Every drop of ink should represent data

Data ink: Ink that represents actual data points
Non-data ink: Gridlines, borders, backgrounds, decorations
Goal: Maximize the ratio of data ink to total ink
Remove chart junk: 3D effects, unnecessary colors, decorative elements
Keep only what serves comprehension

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Default Plot (Cluttered)


Ineffective: Gray background, heavy gridlines, legend requiring eye travel, and borders all compete for attention. The data-to-ink ratio is low - most ink conveys no data.

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Decluttered with Direct Labels


Effective: High data-to-ink ratio achieved by removing backgrounds, excess gridlines, and legend. Direct labels connect to data via proximity (Gestalt principle).

title: Best Practices
text:
Principle 3: Use Preattentive Attributes
Attention with attributes processed in <250ms

Color: Most powerful
Size: Indicates importance
Position: Spatial relationships
Intensity: Bold vs light
Use strategically - don’t dilute attention

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: All Equal (No Focus)


Ineffective: All bars are equal - where should the viewer look? No visual hierarchy means no clear message.

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Strategic Highlighting


Effective: Red instantly draws the eye to the problem. Gray provides context without competing for attention.

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Using Size for Emphasis


Effective: Size combined with color creates a clear hierarchy. The large red point in August demands attention while smaller gray points provide context.

title: Best Practices
text:
Principle 4: Gray and Bold Technique
Use color to highlight, gray to push back

Bold color for what matters most
Gray for supporting context
Maximum one bold color per chart
Creates instant visual hierarchy
Reduces cognitive load

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Too Many Colors


Ineffective: Multiple bold colors fragment attention. When everything demands attention, nothing gets it.

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Gray and Bold Applied


Effective: One bold color directs attention immediately to the problem area. Gray bars provide necessary context without distraction.

title: Best Practices
text:
Principle 5: Think Like a Designer
Visual design principles enhance communication

Accessibility: Colorblind-safe palettes
Alignment: Create invisible structure
White space: Let your data breathe
Contrast: Guide the eye
Typography: Readable, professional fonts

title: Best Practices
text:
Accessibility: Colorblind-Safe Palettes


Always use colorblind-safe palettes. Approximately 8% of men and 0.5% of women have color vision deficiency. Blue-orange combinations work for nearly everyone.

title: Best Practices
text:
Design Principles: Alignment & Spacing


Effective design: Generous margins, aligned text, strategic white space, and clear visual hierarchy make the message instantly clear and professional.

title: Best Practices
text:
Using Annotations Strategically


Annotations tell the story. The chart clearly shows what happened, when it happened, and why it matters - the viewer doesn’t need to guess.

title: Best Practices
text:
Before/After: Design Transformation


Design transformation: horizontal orientation, strategic color, descriptive title, reference line, and clean styling create a professional, focused message.

title: Best Practices
section: Principle 6: Tell a Story with Data
text:
Principle 6: Tell a Story with Data
Transform insights into narrative

Beginning: Set context (current state)
Middle: Show the problem/opportunity
End: Recommend action
Use descriptive titles that state your point
Guide your audience through the data

title: Best Practices
text:
Narrative vs Descriptive Titles


Narrative titles tell the story. The right chart doesn’t just show data - it communicates the achievement and its magnitude immediately.

title: Best Practices
text:
Small Multiples: Powerful Comparisons


Small multiples enable comparison. Same scales across panels make differences immediately visible. Trend lines show improvement rates at a glance.

title: Best Practices
text:
Small Multiples: Distribution Comparisons


Distribution comparison made easy. Procedure C clearly clusters below the target with minimal variation, while Procedure D shows high variability and longer recovery.

title: Best Practices
text:
Complete Story Example


Complete narrative: Beginning (context with peers), middle (intervention and dramatic improvement), end (current state showing success). Every element supports the story.

title: Best Practices
text:
Advanced Topic: Handling Uncertainty


Show uncertainty honestly. Confidence intervals demonstrate that even accounting for variability, the new treatment shows meaningful improvement over the standard.

title: Best Practices
text:
Advanced Topic: Distribution of Uncertainty


Full distribution view. The minimal overlap between distributions shows that the new treatment improvement is robust, not just a result of a few outliers.

title: Best Practices
text:
Advanced Topic: Correlation Matrices


Multivariate relationships at a glance. Correlation matrices reveal complex patterns - here showing BMI and stress as strongest blood pressure predictors.

title: Best Practices
text:
Common Pitfall: Cherry-Picking Time Ranges


Always show full context. The “growth” story disappears when viewing the complete timeline. Cherry-picking ranges is a common way to mislead.

title: Best Practices
section: Edge Case: When Breaking Rules Makes Sense
text:
Edge Case: When Breaking Rules Makes Sense


Breaking the “zero baseline” rule is appropriate when zero is meaningless (temperature, stock prices, pH). The focus should be on clinically meaningful variation.

title: Best Practices
text:
Summary: Six Core Principles

Choose the Right Chart Type - Match visualization to data and message
Eliminate Clutter - Maximize data-to-ink ratio
Use Preattentive Attributes - Guide attention strategically
Apply Gray and Bold - Create visual hierarchy
Think Like a Designer - Professional, accessible presentation
Tell a Story - Transform insights into narrative

title: Best Practices
text:
Key Takeaways

Every choice matters - color, position, size, titles
Less is more - remove everything that doesn’t serve the message
Context is crucial - never cherry-pick data ranges
Accessibility counts - use colorblind-safe palettes
Focus attention - one bold color, clear hierarchy
Tell the story - guide your audience to action

title: Best Practices
text:
When to Break the Rules
Rules are guidelines, not laws

Zero baseline: not for temperature, stock prices, or indices
Pie charts: acceptable for simple two-part comparisons
Multiple colors: when showing categorical data without hierarchy
The test: Does breaking the rule serve your audience better?
Always ask: Am I making the data clearer or just different?

title: Introduction to R
text:
Variables and Data Types

Numeric — numbers such as 3.14, 42
Integer — whole numbers with L suffix, e.g. 5L
Character — text values like "data"
Logical — TRUE or FALSE
Factor — categorical values with levels
Complex — numbers with imaginary parts like 1 + 2i



Show the code
x <- 5          # numeric
name <- "Alice" # character
flag <- TRUE    # logical
colors <- factor(c("red", "blue", "green"))



Variables store values in memory and can be reused later
R is dynamically typed: type depends on the stored value

title: Introduction to R
text:
Vectors and Sequences

Create ordered collections with c() and sequences with seq()
Useful for numeric data, indexes, and repeated values



Show the code
ages <- c(23, 35, 28)
seq(1, 100, 3)
seq(1, 2, length.out = 10)

title: Introduction to R
text:
Factors and Categorical Variables

Store categories or groups with fixed levels
Important for statistical modeling and reporting
Use factor() to make discrete labels or ordered categories



Show the code
gender <- factor(c("Male", "Female", "Male", "Female"),
                 levels = c("Male", "Female"))
physical_activity <- factor(sample(c(1, 2), 10, replace = TRUE),
                            levels = c(1, 2),
                            labels = c("Yes", "No"))

title: Introduction to R
text:
Lists and Matrices


Lists

Store mixed types in one object
Can contain vectors, data frames, functions, or other lists
Good for nested results and complex outputs



Show the code
my_list <- list(name = "Alice", score = 95, data = c(1, 2, 3))



Matrices

Two-dimensional arrays with a single data type
Ideal for numeric calculations, matrices, and linear algebra
Built from vectors using matrix(), cbind(), or rbind()



Show the code
m <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3)

title: Introduction to R
text:
Data Structures

Data frames are the most common table structure in R
They combine columns of equal length and can contain different types
Lists and matrices are also important foundational structures



Show the code
my_data <- data.frame(
  ID = 1:5,
  Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "David", "Eva"),
  Age = sample(20:50, 5, replace = TRUE)
)

Install several packages:

pacman::p_load() installs missing packages and loads them in one command.

Readability

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
What is Grammar of Graphics?

A systematic framework for creating visualizations
Developed by Leland Wilkinson, implemented in ggplot2 by Hadley Wickham
Treats plots as layered compositions of graphical elements
Separates data from aesthetics from geometry
Enables infinite combinations from finite components
More flexible than traditional plotting systems


Core Philosophy: Build complex visualizations by combining simple, well-defined layers

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
Why ggplot2?

Consistent syntax across all plot types
Flexible and extensible - easy to customize
Professional quality output
Reproducible - code-based approach
Large ecosystem of extensions
Industry standard in R community


vs Base R: More intuitive, consistent, and powerful for complex visualizations

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
The Seven Layers of Grammar

Data - The dataset being visualized
Aesthetics - Mapping data to visual properties
Geometries - Visual marks (points, lines, bars)
Statistics - Data transformations and summaries
Coordinates - The plotting space and axes
Facets - Subplots for data subsets
Scales - Mapping data values to aesthetics


Plus: Themes for overall visual styling

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
1. Data Layer
The foundation of every ggplot2 visualization

Must be a data frame or tibble
Each row represents an observation
Each column represents a variable
Data should be in tidy format

Each variable in one column
Each observation in one row
Each value in one cell




Code
# Basic structure
ggplot(data = my_data)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
2. Aesthetics (aes)
Mapping data variables to visual properties

Position: x, y
Color: color (points/lines), fill (areas)
Size: size of points or line width
Shape: point shapes
Transparency: alpha (0 = transparent, 1 = opaque)
Line type: linetype (solid, dashed, dotted)
Group: group (for grouping data)



Code
ggplot(data, aes(x = var1, y = var2, color = var3))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
3. Geometries (geom)
Visual representations of data

geom_point() - Scatter plots
geom_line() - Line graphs
geom_bar() / geom_col() - Bar charts
geom_histogram() - Histograms
geom_boxplot() - Box plots
geom_violin() - Violin plots
geom_smooth() - Smoothed conditional means
And many more…


Key concept: Geoms are added as layers with +

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
4. Statistics (stat)
Data transformations and summaries

Many geoms have default statistics
stat_identity - Use data as-is
stat_count - Count observations
stat_bin - Bin data into groups
stat_smooth - Add smoothed line
stat_summary - Compute summary statistics


Usually implicit: Most geoms automatically apply appropriate statistics

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
5. Coordinates (coord)
Defining the plotting space

coord_cartesian() - Default Cartesian coordinates
coord_flip() - Flip x and y axes
coord_polar() - Polar coordinates
coord_fixed() - Fixed aspect ratio
coord_trans() - Transformed coordinates



Code
# Flip axes for horizontal bars
ggplot(data, aes(x = category, y = value)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip()

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
6. Facets
Creating subplots for data subsets

facet_wrap() - Wrap panels by one variable
facet_grid() - Grid of panels by two variables
Useful for comparing groups
Can have free or fixed scales



Code
# Facet by one variable
facet_wrap(~ treatment_group)

# Facet by two variables
facet_grid(gender ~ region)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
7. Scales
Mapping data values to aesthetic properties

Control how data maps to aesthetics
scale_x_continuous() - Continuous x-axis
scale_color_manual() - Manual color specification
scale_fill_brewer() - ColorBrewer palettes
scale_y_log10() - Logarithmic transformation
Control breaks, limits, labels, transformations



Code
scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue", "green"))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
8. Guides (Legends & Axes)
Helping readers interpret the plot

Axes: Show scale of position aesthetics
Legends: Show scale of other aesthetics (color, size, shape)
Controlled by guides() function
Can be positioned, styled, or removed
Automatically generated from aesthetics



Code
guides(color = guide_legend(title = "Treatment Group"))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
Building Plots Progressively
The power of layering

ggplot(data, aes(x = age, y = systolic_bp)) +        # 1. Data + aesthetics
  geom_point() +                                       # 2. Add points
  geom_smooth() +                                      # 3. Add trend line
  facet_wrap(~ treatment_group) +                      # 4. Add facets
  theme_minimal()                                      # 5. Apply theme


Each layer builds on the previous, creating complex visualizations from simple components

Color Theory Basics

Hue: The color itself (red, blue, green)
Saturation: Intensity/purity of color
Luminance: Brightness/lightness
Contrast: Difference between colors


Key principles: - Use color purposefully, not decoratively - Ensure sufficient contrast for readability - Consider colorblind accessibility (~8% of males, ~0.5% of females) - Limit number of colors (typically ≤7 for categorical data)

Best Practices for Color

Use color purposefully - not just for decoration
Prefer colorblind-safe palettes - viridis, ColorBrewer, paletteer curated sets
Limit colors - typically ≤7 distinct colors for categorical
Use redundant encoding - combine color with shape, pattern, or position
Ensure contrast - especially for text and important distinctions
Consider grayscale - will it work if printed in black & white?
Cultural context - red/green may have different meanings
Test with target audience - especially for accessibility needs

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
Creating an Organizational Theme


Code
# Hospital/Clinical Report Theme
theme_clinical_report <- function(base_size = 12, base_family = "serif") {
  theme_bw(base_size = base_size, base_family = base_family) +
  theme(
    # Professional serif fonts
    text = element_text(family = base_family),
    
    # Plot titles - centered and bold
    plot.title = element_text(size = base_size * 1.3, face = "bold", 
                              hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = base_size * 1.1, hjust = 0.5,
                                 color = "gray30", margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9, hjust = 1,
                                face = "italic", color = "gray50"),
    
    # Axis elements - clear and readable
    axis.title = element_text(size = base_size * 1.1, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9, color = "gray20"),
    axis.line = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    
    # Panel - clean with subtle grid
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "gray90", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "gray40", fill = NA, linewidth = 1),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    
    # Legend - bottom position, horizontal
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(size = base_size, face = "bold"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    legend.key = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    
    # Plot background
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)
  )
}

title: Data Analysis
text:
Why Check Normality?
Many parametric tests (t-test, ANOVA, Pearson’s r) assume normally distributed data.
Failing to check normality can lead to:

Invalid p-values
Wrong test selection
Misleading conclusions

Two approaches: Visual methods + Statistical tests

title: Data Analysis
text:
Visual Methods — Histogram

hist(
  p$age_of_participants,
  main  = "Histogram with Density Line",
  xlab  = "Age",
  ylab  = "Density",
  col   = "grey",
  border = "black",
  freq  = FALSE
)
lines(density(p$age_of_participants), col = "red", lwd = 2)


A roughly bell-shaped curve suggests normality. Skewed or multimodal histograms indicate non-normality.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Visual Methods — QQ Plot

qqnorm(p$sbp_in_mm_hg, main = "Q-Q Plot: SBP")
qqline(p$sbp_in_mm_hg, col = "red")


Points should follow the red diagonal line closely if the data are normally distributed. Deviations at the tails indicate non-normality.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Statistical Tests — Shapiro-Wilk
Best for small samples (n ≤ 50). Randomly sample if n > 50.

p1 <- p[sample(nrow(p), 50), ]
s_test <- shapiro.test(p1$age_of_participants)
s_test


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  p1$age_of_participants
W = 0.92804, p-value = 0.004662



Interpretation: p > 0.05 → data does not significantly deviate from normality (cannot reject H₀ of normality).

title: Data Analysis
text:
Statistical Tests — Kolmogorov-Smirnov
Suitable for larger samples. Compares distribution to a theoretical normal.

ks_test <- ks.test(p$sbp_in_mm_hg, "pnorm",
                   mean = mean(p$sbp_in_mm_hg),
                   sd   = sd(p$sbp_in_mm_hg))
ks_test


    Asymptotic one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  p$sbp_in_mm_hg
D = 0.052082, p-value = 0.06522
alternative hypothesis: two-sided



Note: Use options(scipen = 999) to display p-values in decimal format instead of scientific notation.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit — 1 Group
Tests whether the observed distribution matches an expected distribution.

observed <- table(p$ever_screened_for_bp)
total    <- sum(observed)
expected <- c(1/2, 1/2) * total

chisq_test <- chisq.test(x = observed, p = expected / sum(expected))
chisq_test


    Chi-squared test for given probabilities

data:  observed
X-squared = 80.23, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16



Assumption: Expected frequency ≥ 5 in each cell.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Chi-Square Test — 2 Binary Groups (Expected ≥ 5)
Tests association between two categorical variables using a contingency table.

table_gender_dm <- table(p$sex_of_participants, p$past_history_of_diabetes)
table_gender_dm

        
          no yes
  female 332  17
  male   265  17

chisq_m5 <- chisq.test(table_gender_dm, correct = FALSE)
chisq_m5


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  table_gender_dm
X-squared = 0.40978, df = 1, p-value = 0.5221

# Check expected frequencies
chisq_m5$expected

        
               no      yes
  female 330.1949 18.80507
  male   266.8051 15.19493



Use correct = FALSE to apply the standard Pearson Chi-square (no Yates correction).

title: Data Analysis
text:
Chi-Square — Yates Continuity Correction
Yates correction subtracts 0.5 from the absolute difference between observed and expected frequency before squaring.

# With Yates correction (correct = TRUE is default for 2x2 tables)
chisq.test(table_gender_dm, correct = TRUE)


    Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction

data:  table_gender_dm
X-squared = 0.2142, df = 1, p-value = 0.6435



Apply when sample sizes are small or expected frequencies approach 5.

title: Data Analysis
text:
When Expected Frequency < 5
Two options: Monte Carlo simulation or Fisher’s Exact Test.

table_htn_dm <- table(p$ever_screened_for_bp, p$past_history_of_diabetes)

# Monte Carlo simulation (B = number of replicates, min p = 1/(B+1))
chisq_mc <- chisq.test(table_htn_dm, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 2000)
chisq_mc


    Pearson's Chi-squared test with simulated p-value (based on 2000
    replicates)

data:  table_htn_dm
X-squared = 11.381, df = NA, p-value = 0.0004998

# Fisher's Exact Test
fisher_test <- fisher.test(table_htn_dm)
fisher_test


    Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data

p-value = 0.0002606
alternative hypothesis: true odds ratio is not equal to 1

title: Data Analysis
text:
One Group — Z Test
Use when population SD is known and n > 30.

pr  <- p |> filter(wealth_index_of_participants == "richer")
mu  <- mean(p$age_of_participants)
sigma <- sd(p$age_of_participants)

s_mean <- mean(pr$age_of_participants)
n      <- length(pr$age_of_participants)
z      <- (s_mean - mu) / (sigma / sqrt(n))

p_two_tailed     <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z)))
p_one_tailed_gt  <- 1 - pnorm(z)
p_one_tailed_lt  <- pnorm(z)

cat("Z =", round(z, 3),
    "\nTwo-tailed p =", round(p_two_tailed, 4),
    "\nOne-tailed (greater) p =", round(p_one_tailed_gt, 4))

Z = -0.879 
Two-tailed p = 0.3794 
One-tailed (greater) p = 0.8103

title: Debugging Plots
text:
Debugging plots are essential tools for diagnosing issues in data visualization and analysis. They help identify problems such as incorrect data representation, scaling issues, or unexpected patterns in the data. In this guide, we will explore various techniques and tools for creating effective debugging plots.





Missing or incorrect data types
# Check data types
str(mtcars)

# Check for missing values
sum(is.na(mtcars))

# Visualize missing patterns
library(naniar)
vis_miss(mtcars)
Outliers affecting scales
# Check for outliers
boxplot(mtcars$mpg)

# Use robust statistics
library(robustbase)
summary(mtcars$mpg)





Mapping vs Setting Aesthetics
# Correct: Map color to variable
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point()

# Incorrect: Setting color globally
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = "red")  # This sets all points to red
Factor Level Issues
# Check factor levels
levels(mtcars$cyl)

# Reorder factors if needed
mtcars$cyl <- factor(mtcars$cyl, levels = c("4", "6", "8"))
Geom Conflicts
# Error: Can't use geom_bar with y aesthetic
# ggplot(data, aes(x = category, y = value)) + geom_bar()

# Correct: Use stat = "identity"
ggplot(data, aes(x = category, y = value)) + 
  geom_bar(stat = "identity")







# Check ggplot object structure
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
str(p)

# View plot data
p$data
p$mapping



# Build plot incrementally
p1 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg))
print(p1)  # Should show empty plot

p2 <- p1 + geom_point()
print(p2)  # Check if points appear

p3 <- p2 + theme_minimal()
print(p3)  # Check theme application



# Enable ggplot2 debugging
options(ggplot2.debug = TRUE)

# Check for warnings
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()






# Problem: Length mismatch
# ggplot(data, aes(x = x_var, y = y_var, color = short_vector))

# Solution: Ensure vectors are same length or use single values
ggplot(data, aes(x = x_var, y = y_var, color = factor(category)))



# Problem: Wrong scale type
# ggplot(data, aes(x = factor_var, y = numeric_var)) + scale_x_continuous()

# Solution: Use appropriate scale
ggplot(data, aes(x = factor_var, y = numeric_var)) + scale_x_discrete()



# Problem: Typo in parameter name
# geom_point(size = 3)  # Correct
# geom_point(siz = 3)   # Incorrect

# Solution: Check documentation
?geom_point






# Residual plots for model diagnostics
model <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
plot(model)

# QQ plots for normality
qqnorm(mtcars$mpg)
qqline(mtcars$mpg)



# Correlation plots
library(corrplot)
corrplot(cor(mtcars))

# Pairs plots
pairs(mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "hp")])



# Plot data distributions
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg)) + 
  geom_histogram() + 
  facet_wrap(~ cyl)

# Check for data issues
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_text(aes(label = rownames(mtcars)), check_overlap = TRUE)






# When plot fails
tryCatch({
  ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
}, error = function(e) {
  print(e)
  traceback()
})



library(profvis)

# Profile plotting code
profvis({
  p <- ggplot(large_dataset, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point()
  print(p)
})



# Check memory usage
gc()

# For large datasets, use sampling
sample_data <- mtcars[sample(nrow(mtcars), 1000, replace = TRUE), ]
ggplot(sample_data, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()

title: Plotting Tools
text:
This chapter introduces various tools and libraries available in R for creating visualizations. It covers base R plotting functions, as well as popular packages like ggplot2 and lattice, which offer advanced capabilities for creating complex and customizable plots.


R’s built-in plotting functions provide a solid foundation for data visualization:


# Scatter plot
plot(x = mtcars$wt, y = mtcars$mpg,
     xlab = "Weight", ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
     main = "Scatter Plot Example")

# Line plot
plot(x = 1:10, y = (1:10)^2, type = "l",
     xlab = "X", ylab = "Y^2")

# Bar plot
barplot(height = c(10, 15, 8, 12),
        names.arg = c("A", "B", "C", "D"))

# Histogram
hist(mtcars$mpg, breaks = 10,
     xlab = "Miles per Gallon",
     main = "Histogram of MPG")



# Multiple plots in one window
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))  # 2x2 grid

plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
hist(mtcars$mpg)
boxplot(mtcars$mpg ~ mtcars$cyl)
plot(density(mtcars$mpg))

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))  # Reset to single plot




ggplot2 is the most popular R package for data visualization, based on the Grammar of Graphics:


library(ggplot2)

# Basic scatter plot
ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point()

# Adding aesthetics
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(title = "MPG vs Weight by Cylinders",
       x = "Weight (1000 lbs)",
       y = "Miles per Gallon")



# Points, lines, bars
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg))

p + geom_point()           # Scatter plot
p + geom_smooth()          # Smooth line
p + geom_line()            # Line plot
p + geom_bar(stat = "identity")  # Bar plot
p + geom_histogram()       # Histogram
p + geom_boxplot()         # Box plot



# Faceting
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ cyl) +
  theme_minimal()

# Custom themes
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("Custom Theme Example")




Lattice provides trellis graphics for multivariate data:
library(lattice)

# Scatter plot matrix
splom(mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "hp")])

# Conditional plots
xyplot(mpg ~ wt | factor(cyl), data = mtcars,
       layout = c(3, 1))

# 3D plots
cloud(mpg ~ wt * hp, data = mtcars)





library(plotly)

# Convert ggplot to interactive
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
ggplotly(p)

# Native plotly
plot_ly(mtcars, x = ~wt, y = ~mpg, type = "scatter", mode = "markers")



library(ggvis)

# Interactive ggplot2-like syntax
mtcars %>%
  ggvis(x = ~wt, y = ~mpg) %>%
  layer_points() %>%
  add_tooltip(function(df) paste("Weight:", df$wt, "MPG:", df$mpg))






library(ggstatsplot)

# Statistical plots with tests
ggbetweenstats(data = mtcars, x = cyl, y = mpg)



library(ggplot2)
library(maps)

# Basic map
world <- map_data("world")
ggplot(world, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) +
  geom_polygon(fill = "lightblue", color = "black")



library(igraph)
library(ggraph)

# Create network
g <- make_ring(10)
ggraph(g, layout = "circle") +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point(size = 5)





Base R: Quick plots, statistical graphics
ggplot2: Publication-quality static plots, complex customizations
Lattice: Multivariate data, trellis displays
plotly/ggvis: Interactive web-based visualizations
Specialized packages: Domain-specific visualizations (maps, networks, etc.)

Keep it simple: Avoid clutter, focus on the message

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggstatsplot is an R package that combines statistical tests and publication-ready visualisations in a single function call. Each plot automatically selects, runs, and annotates the appropriate statistical test based on your data, displaying results directly on the figure.
This removes a common workflow bottleneck: running a test in one place, building a plot in another, and manually annotating results.

install.packages("ggstatsplot")
library(ggstatsplot)

Why use it?

One function produces both the visual and the statistical result
Automatically annotates effect sizes and confidence intervals
Sensible defaults — works out of the box for most common comparisons
Output is a ggplot2 object, so you can add layers or themes as usual

Function

ggbetweenstats()

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggbetweenstats() — Group Comparisons
Use this when you want to compare a continuous variable across two or more independent groups.

library(ggstatsplot)

# Compare systolic BP across fuel type groups
ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = fuel_type,         # grouping variable (categorical)
  y     = sbp_0m,            # outcome variable (continuous)
  title = "Systolic BP by Fuel Type"
)

What the output shows:

A violin + boxplot combination with individual data points
The statistical test used (Welch’s ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis, chosen automatically)
The p-value, effect size (η² or ε²), and confidence interval
Pairwise comparisons (if more than 2 groups)

Choosing parametric vs non-parametric:

# Force non-parametric (Kruskal-Wallis)
ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = fuel_type,
  y     = sbp_0m,
  type  = "nonparametric"   # "parametric", "nonparametric", "robust", "bayes"
)

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggscatterstats() — Correlation
Use this when you want to examine the relationship between two continuous variables.

ggscatterstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = current_age,
  y     = sbp_0m,
  title = "Age vs Systolic BP at Baseline"
)

What the output shows:

A scatter plot with a linear trend line and confidence band
Pearson (or Spearman) correlation coefficient, r
p-value and 95% confidence interval for r
Marginal histograms on both axes

Using Spearman instead of Pearson:

ggscatterstats(
  data = overall_up,
  x    = current_age,
  y    = sbp_0m,
  type = "nonparametric"   # uses Spearman's rho
)

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
gghistostats() — Distribution
Use this when you want to visualise the distribution of a single continuous variable with a one-sample test.

gghistostats(
  data     = overall_up,
  x        = current_age,
  title    = "Distribution of Age at Enrolment",
  test.value = 40          # hypothesised population mean
)

What the output shows:

Histogram with overlaid density curve
One-sample t-test (or Wilcoxon signed-rank) against the specified test.value
Mean, median, and their confidence intervals

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
Reading the statistical annotation
Every ggstatsplot figure includes a subtitle with the test results in a standardised format:
Welch's ANOVA, F(2, 147.3) = 5.23, p = 0.006, ω² = 0.06, 95% CI [0.01, 0.14]



Component
Meaning




Test name
Which test was used (selected automatically)


Test statistic
F, t, χ², H etc.


p-value
Statistical significance


Effect size
Practical significance (ω², d, r, etc.)


95% CI
Uncertainty around the effect size









TipInterpreting effect sizes




η² / ω²: Small ≈ 0.01, Medium ≈ 0.06, Large ≈ 0.14 (for ANOVA)
Cohen’s d: Small ≈ 0.2, Medium ≈ 0.5, Large ≈ 0.8 (for t-tests)
r: Small ≈ 0.1, Medium ≈ 0.3, Large ≈ 0.5 (for correlation)

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Parameterised Reports
Parameters let you run the same document with different inputs — for example, generating one report per hospital, intervention group, or region.

1. Declare parameters in the YAML header
---
title: "Site Report"
params:
  site_name: "Site A"
  intervention: "Control"
---


2. Use parameters in code

# params$site_name and params$intervention are available as R objects
site_data <- overall_up |>
  filter(site == params$site_name,
         intervention == params$intervention)

nrow(site_data)



3. Render with different parameter values

# Render from R for a specific site
quarto::quarto_render(
  input  = "site_report.qmd",
  output_file = "site_a_report.html",
  execute_params = list(
    site_name    = "Site A",
    intervention = "Intervention"
  )
)



4. Batch render — one file per site

library(purrr)

sites <- c("Site A", "Site B", "Site C")

walk(sites, \(site) {
  quarto::quarto_render(
    input          = "site_report.qmd",
    output_file    = paste0(tolower(gsub(" ", "_", site)), "_report.html"),
    execute_params = list(site_name = site)
  )
})

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Inline R Code
Embedding computed values directly in text avoids copy-paste errors and keeps your document reproducible.
Syntax:
200

# In a code chunk (runs silently):
n_total  <- nrow(overall_up)
mean_age <- round(mean(overall_up$current_age, na.rm = TRUE), 1)

In Quarto prose:
The study enrolled 200 participants with a mean age of
NA years (SD = 14.3).
Rendered output:

The study enrolled 1 248 participants with a mean age of 38.4 years (SD = 11.2).







Tip



Compute all summary values in one early code chunk marked #| include: false, then reference them via inline code throughout the document.

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Cross-References
Cross-references auto-number figures and tables and create clickable links.

Figures
Add a label that starts with fig- and a fig-cap:
```{r}
#| label: fig-sbp-hist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of baseline systolic blood pressure."
ggplot(overall_up, aes(x = sbp_0m)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(x = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", y = "Count")
```
Reference in text: @fig-sbp-hist → renders as “Figure 1”


Tables
Add a label starting with tbl- and a tbl-cap:
```{r}
#| label: tbl-demographics
#| tbl-cap: "Baseline characteristics of study participants."
library(gtsummary)
overall_up |>
  select(current_age, sex, tobacco_type, fuel_type) |>
  tbl_summary()
```
Reference in text: @tbl-demographics → renders as “Table 1”

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Multiple Output Formats
One .qmd file can produce HTML, PDF, and Word output.
---
title: "Study Report"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    theme: flatly
  pdf:
    toc: true
    number-sections: true
  docx:
    toc: true
---
Render all formats at once:
quarto render study_report.qmd






WarningPDF requirements



PDF rendering requires a LaTeX installation. Install tinytex from R:
install.packages("tinytex")
tinytex::install_tinytex()
